blocks.text: Imagine a world where anyone could directly change the internal state of your objects, potentially breaking their intended functionality. How can we prevent this chaos?

blocks.markdown: Encapsulation is a fundamental concept in object-oriented programming that helps protect the internal state of an object. By bundling the data (state) and the methods (operations) that operate on the data into a single unit, we can control how the data is accessed and modified. This is achieved through the use of class invariants and visibility modifiers.

blocks.title: Class Invariant
blocks.text: A class invariant is a condition that must always hold true for an object of the class, except during the execution of a method.

blocks.markdown: A class invariant is typically established by the constructor of the class and is maintained by ensuring that all methods preserve the invariant. This ensures that the object remains in a valid state throughout its lifetime.

blocks.title: Establishing a Class Invariant
blocks.prompt: Consider a class `Rectangle` that represents a rectangle with a width and a height. The invariant is that both width and height must be positive.

steps.text: Define the class `Rectangle` with private attributes for width and height.
Use a constructor to initialize the width and height, ensuring they are positive.
Provide methods to access and modify the width and height, ensuring they maintain the invariant.

blocks.title: Visibility Modifiers
blocks.text: Visibility modifiers such as `private`, `protected`, and `public` control access to class members. Use them to enforce encapsulation.

blocks.markdown: By marking class attributes as `private`, we prevent external code from directly accessing and modifying them. Instead, access is controlled through public methods, which can enforce the class invariant.

blocks.title: Using Visibility Modifiers
blocks.prompt: Modify the `Rectangle` class to demonstrate how visibility modifiers protect its invariant.

steps.text: Ensure width and height are private.
Provide public methods to access and modify width and height.
Ensure these methods maintain the invariant.

blocks.markdown: Returning a reference to internal mutable state can break encapsulation. If external code modifies this state, it can violate the class invariant.

blocks.title: Danger of Returning Mutable References
blocks.text: Avoid returning references to mutable internal objects. Instead, return copies or immutable views.
